planting.note: Wait until soil is thoroughly warm, since lima beans rot quickly in cold, wet ground; sow at a trellis base once frost danger has fully passed.

directions: This vigorous pole lima traces to seed kept by members of the Potawatomi Nation and later preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network. Vines climb 8 to 10 feet and need a sturdy trellis or pole, rewarding the support with a heavy set of pods best picked for fresh shelling or left to dry for storage beans. It tolerates cooler summer nights better than many lima types, making it a dependable choice outside the deep South. Give plants full sun and even moisture through pod set for the best yields.

planting.note: Direct sow at the base of corn stalks once soil has warmed, in the traditional Three Sisters style, so vines can climb the stalks as they grow.

directions: A traditional Cherokee heirloom grown interplanted with corn, this pole bean produces earth-toned seeds mottled in tan, brown, and maroon patterns that seed keepers have long kept as a single mixed population rather than sorting by color. Pods can be eaten young as snap beans, picked at the shell stage for a quick-cooking fresh bean, or left to dry fully for winter storage. Vines need 8 feet or more of support, whether that is a trellis, teepee of poles, or standing corn stalks. It is a dependable, disease-tolerant bean well suited to humid eastern gardens.

planting.note: Sow in warm soil after frost danger has passed; this desert-adapted bean tolerates heat far better than cold, wet conditions.

directions: Maintained for generations by Hopi farmers in the arid Southwest, this bush-type lima bears brilliant orange-and-burgundy mottled seeds that dry to a muted brown. It is notably drought and heat tolerant, reflecting centuries of selection for dryland farming on the Hopi mesas, and is traditionally parched and ground into a flour-like meal as well as cooked whole. Plants are more compact than many pole limas, making them workable in smaller garden beds. Harvest pods as they dry for the fullest flavor and best storage quality.

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks rather than single rows for reliable wind pollination once soil has warmed well past the last frost.

directions: Tama Flint is the traditional corn of the Meskwaki (Mesquakie) people of the Meskwaki Settlement near Tama, Iowa, grown there for generations without irrigation or synthetic inputs. Ears carry eight rows of hard, flint-type kernels in shades of red, blue, and purple, prized for grinding into meal and for corn soup. A related Meskwaki corn called Sac Blue is deep red and white, and the two are often grown and preserved side by side as part of ongoing tribal seed-saving efforts. Because flint corn cross-pollinates readily, isolate plantings from other corn to keep the line true.

planting.note: Plant in blocks of at least four short rows once the soil has warmed, to ensure even wind pollination of the ears.

directions: Also known as Fairfax Brown, this flour corn is stewarded by the Osage Nation, whose farmers historically grew it in the river valleys of the Ozark region. Plants are relatively compact for a flour corn and typically set one or two ears per stalk, with kernels in a deep, chocolate brown that make it as ornamental as it is useful. The soft starch kernels grind easily into cornmeal with a rich, nutty flavor. Save ears from the strongest, most true-to-type plants each year to keep the line distinct from other corn types grown nearby.

planting.note: Plant in blocks once soil is reliably warm; this rare flour corn benefits from hand-pollination care to preserve its distinctive kernel pattern.

directions: This flour corn was collected in the mid-20th century from the Osage Reservation in northern Oklahoma and takes its name from the striking mix of blue, white, and bronze kernels spotted and splashed across each cob. Stalks stay relatively short for a flour corn, generally setting two ears of four to six inches per plant. Because it is a rare, endangered heirloom with few seed keepers maintaining it, isolating plantings from other corn varieties helps protect its unusual coloring for future seed saving. Grind dried kernels into cornmeal or display whole ears for their ornamental speckling.
